newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Tsumeb copper miners to return to work.
newsitem.headline: Tsumeb copper miners to return to work.

text.p: Workers at Tsumeb Corporation Ltd's (TCL) copper mine will return to work next week for the first time since a crippling six-week strike ended earlier this month, owners Gold Fields of Namibia said.

But when workers return to the mine, about 800 of them will be retrenched under an agreement reached between mine management and the Mineworkers Union of Namibia, Gold Fields spokesman Dermot Whyte told Reuters on Thursday.
"We sent everybody home, they will be returning to the mine on Monday and then they will be told who will be retrenched and who will keep their jobs," Whyte said by telephone from Namibia.
He said repairs to TCL's copper smelter, which was badly damaged during the strike, were still under way.
"The mines will hopefully begin working at the beginning of December," Whyte added.

TCL general manager Tony de Beer said management regretted not being able to keep employment at current levels but cited the strike, which cost the company in excess of N$1 million a day, and the depressed world copper price as reasons for the sackings.

"All employees affected by the reduction of our labour force will be first in line for re-employment if circumstances are such that TCL is once again in a position to employ additional workers," de Beer said in a statement.

De Beer said the damage to the smelter and infrastructure had had an adverse efffect on TCL's financial position. The company had brought forward a decision to close one of TCL's shafts as a result of the strike.
The three mines making up TCL, Otjihase, Kombat and Tsumeb, and smelters have been shut down since August 23.
The strike cost TCL some 80 tonnes a day in lost copper production and a similar amount in lost lead.
TCL produced just under 30,000 tonnes of blister copper last year and 27,000 tonnes of lead. Most of the lead was produced from bought-in material while copper output was from TCL mines.
